Succinctly stated, the case of the Prosecution is that on 04.04.2018, an information was received at PS regarding admission of victim Ms. 'R' in the GTB Hospital; that IO went to the hospital and obtained her MLC on which Doctor has mentioned A/H/O Trauma to head by self banging of head to wall as stated by her husband/accused and patient was unconscious and during treatment, victim died.

It is alleged in the statement of the complainant, Sh. Karan Singh, father of the deceased, that his daughter had entered into a love marriage with the accused Rahul Kumar Thakur; the marriage was cordial in its initial days, however, after some time, the accused Rahul Kumar Thakur began pressurizing his daughter (deceased) to bring money from her parental home, therefore, for the sake of his daughter's happiness and marital harmony, he provided financial assistance to the accused on several occasions.

It is stated that on 04.04.2018, on the receipt of information regarding ill health of his daughter, who was admitted in GTB Hospital, the complainant sent his wife Chandrakanta alongwith his another son-in-law Sachin Thakur to the GTB Hospital; Sachin Thakur informed him that his daughter was seriously ill and he was informed by the Doctor that her daughter was unconscious and had suffered injuries on her head.

The complainant has alleged that his daughter was being beaten by her husband/accused Rahul;
that her daughter was brave and could not have banged her head against a wall.

On the basis of these allegations, the complainant has asserted that his son-in-law Rahul Kumar Thakur, along with his friend Ankit and his wife Namrata, who were staying with the accused for approximately one week prior to the incident, have committed the murder of his daughter Rashmi.

On the basis of statement of the complainant Sh. Karan Singh, present case FIR was registered and the investigation of the matter was conducted.

INVESTIGATION & OTHER PROCEEDINGS 2.

On appearance, in compliance of section 207 Cr.PC, copy of Chargesheet was supplied to the accused and since offences punishable U/s 304 B IPC and 302 IPC are exclusively triable by the Court of Sessions, the present case was committed to this Court.

Charge under Section 498A, 304B IPC and an alternate Charge under Section 302 IPC was framed against the accused Rahul Kumar Thakur, same was read over and explained to him in vernacular, to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.

It was then concluded :
1. Opinion regarding cause of death :
Death in this case occurred as a result of Brain Damage consequent upon blunt force trauma to the head.
2. Opinion regarding manner of death :
(i) given the circumstances of the case, the manner of death in this case assumes great importance as compared to the opinion regarding cause of death.
(ii) The injuries are consistent with an event in which the moving head impacted against a hard surface.
(iii) The head injury could have occurred in a fall or forceful impact of the head against the hard surface like a wall.
Such a forceful impact could have been inflicted by another person in a homicidal assault or self inflicted.
The fall could have been accidental or occurred falling an assault.

(iv) Definitive conclusion regarding the manner of death is a matter of thorough and detailed investigation and co-relation of all evidences (including circumstantial and corroborative) by the investigating authorities.

3. Directions to the investigating agency :
(i) The police are to submit detailed statements from all the concerned parties.
(ii) Any previous medical history / record of use of antipsychotic drugs should be investigated and relevant documents should be furnished.
(iii) The following documents/evidences are to be furnished to the medical board.
(a) Medical record of previous illness / surgery / hospitalization.
 (b) Crime scene investigation report.

The presumption under Section 113B of Indian Evidence Act comes into play only when the following conditions are met:
(i) The death of the woman occurred within seven years of marriage.
(ii) That soon before her death, such woman has been subjected by the accused to cruelty or harassment.
(iii) Such cruelty or harassment should be for or in connection with any demand of dowry.
A close, careful and methodical examination of the evidence on record is required before recording any finding with respect to the charges under Sections 304-B, 498-A IPC and the alternate charge under Section 302 IPC.
The Prosecution case must stand or fall on its own strength and cannot derive support from conjectures, assumptions or emotional considerations arising out of the unfortunate death of a young woman.
None of the Prosecution witnesses have alleged that any dowry was demanded at or before the time of marriage.
No list of dowry articles has been produced, no contemporaneous complaint has been shown, and no independent witness has been examined to support the allegation of any dowry demand.
The evidence clearly reflects that the accused entered into marriage with the deceased fully conscious of her physical condition and did so of his own volition, without raising any demand for dowry either at or before the marriage.
In the ordinary course of human conduct and probabilities, it appears implausible that a person who voluntarily enters into a love marriage with a specially-abled woman, without seeking dowry, would thereafter subject her to harassment or cruelty on account of dowry.
Such an allegation, in the absence of any cogent supporting material, runs contrary to common human behaviour.
Significantly, the Prosecution has failed to place on record any credible circumstance, intervening event or contemporaneous conduct which could reasonably explain the alleged shift in the conduct of the accused from one of acceptance and voluntary commitment to one of dowry-driven harassment.
19 . The alleged monetary demands referred to by PW-1, PW-2, PW-3 and PW-4, upon careful scrutiny, do not satisfy the legal definition of dowry demand.
A holistic reading of their testimonies shows that the amounts allegedly given were towards payment of house rent, purchase of a scooter,
petrol expenses and medical treatment.
Significantly, even with regard to the alleged amount given for purchase of a scooty, it has come on record that the accused ultimately purchased the scooter on installments, which is an admitted fact.
The financial assistance, arising out of post-marital economic constraints or domestic necessities, cannot be equated with dowry demand in the absence of a clear and direct nexus with the marriage.
It is well settled that every demand for money or financial help/aid does not amount to dowry demand within the meaning of Section 304-B IPC.
In the present case, the Prosecution has failed to establish any such nexus between the alleged monetary transactions, including the amount allegedly given for the scooter, and the marriage, thereby falling short of proving an essential ingredient of the offence.
Despite having both the capacity and opportunity to voice any grievance, no allegation of dowry-related harassment or cruelty was ever disclosed by her to any authority or even formally to her family members.
This prolonged and unexplained silence assumes significant evidentiary value and casts a doubt on the prosecution narrative.
The allegations of dowry demand and cruelty, therefore, appear to be retrospective inferences drawn after the unfortunate death of the deceased, which, however sympathetic the circumstances may be, cannot substitute the requirement of proof beyond reasonable doubt in a criminal trial.
A careful examination of the testimonies of all the prosecution witnesses reveals that none of them has been able to point out any specific incident of dowry-related cruelty or harassment which was proximate in time to the date of occurrence.
The allegations made are general and relate to unspecified periods of the marital life, without any clear indication of temporal proximity to the death.
Such vague and stale allegations, unconnected to the immediate circumstances preceding the death, do not satisfy the mandatory requirement of "soon before death" as contemplated under Section 304-B IPC.
In the absence of a live, proximate and direct link between the alleged cruelty and the death of the deceased, the statutory presumption under Section 113-B of the Indian Evidence Act does not arise.
The prosecution has not been able to establish any wilful conduct on the part of the accused of such a nature as was likely to drive the deceased to commit suicide or to cause grave injury to her life, limb or health, nor has it proved any harassment with a view to coercing the deceased or her family members to meet any unlawful demand.
The evidence led by the prosecution, at best, reflects instances of ordinary domestic discord or financial stress, which, even if assumed to be true, do not constitute "cruelty" within the meaning of Section 498-A IPC.
This independent and neutral testimony directly contradicts the prosecution allegation of persistent cruelty and harassment and lends credible support to the defence version, thereby further weakening the Prosecution case under Section 498-A IPC.
23.
There are no injuries on the face of the deceased.
A careful consideration of the medical and factual evidence on record further shows that the mere presence of bruises on the body of the deceased cannot, by itself, be treated as conclusive proof of assault by the accused.
Bruises are a common form of blunt-force injury and can be caused in a variety of circumstances, including accidental impact, pressure/force applied during lifting or handling of the body, friction against hard or semi-hard surfaces, or force exerted in an emergency situation.
In the present case, the evidence shows that after the deceased became unconscious, she was immediately lifted and rushed to the hospital in an emergent situation.
In such circumstances, it is entirely plausible that bruises even though not occurred through chunni, could have occurred while grabbing the deceased through the chest or arms to support her weight or her body might have hit the wall or any part of vehicle while carrying her down from the third floor, or while positioning her on a vehicle for transportation to the hospital.
The defence version that such bruises might have occurred during the process of lifting and rushing the deceased for medical treatment, therefore, cannot be completely ruled out.
The non-production of the statement of a material eye-witness, coupled with the failure to place crucial medical records on record, reflects a lack of due diligence and casts a serious doubt on the fairness and completeness of the investigation.
This opinion that foreful impact could be homicidal or self-inflicted clearly indicates that the medical evidence does not rule out the possibility of self-inflicted injury and, in fact, keeps open multiple plausible explanations.
In the absence of a clear and unequivocal medical opinion pointing towards homicidal death, the prosecution has failed to discharge its burden of proving the offence under Section 302 IPC beyond reasonable doubt.
When the entire evidence is evaluated cumulatively, it becomes evident that the prosecution has failed to prove the essential ingredients of Sections 304-B and 498-A IPC and has also failed to establish homicidal death so as to attract Section 302 IPC.
The evidence on record gives rise to multiple reasonable doubts at every crucial stage.
It is a settled principle of criminal law that suspicion, however strong, cannot take the place of proof and that where two views are possible, the one favouring the accused must be adopted.
28. It is time cherished principle of criminal jurisprudence that if two views are possible on the evidence adduced in the case, one pointing to the guilt of the accused and the other to his innocence,
the view which is favourable to the accused should be adopted.
In cases where the court entertains reasonable doubt regarding the guilt of the accused the benefit of such doubt should go in favour of the accused.
At the same time,
the court must not reject the evidence of the prosecution taking it as false, untrustworthy or unreliable on fanciful grounds or on the basis of conjectures and surmises.
The case of the prosecution must be judged as a whole having regard to the totality of the evidence.
In appreciating the evidence the approach of the court must be integrated not truncated or isolated.
29. In view of the foregoing discussion and upon a cumulative assessment of the entire evidence on record, this Court is of the considered opinion that the Prosecution has failed to discharge its burden of proving the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt.
The evidence led does not establish the foundational facts necessary to attract Sections 304-B or 498-A IPC, nor does it prove that the death of the deceased was homicidal so as to sustain the alternate charge under Section 302 IPC.
On the contrary, the material on record reveals serious inconsistencies, unexplained investigative lapses and multiple plausible explanations consistent with innocence.
The Prosecution case is founded largely on post-event assumptions, vague allegations and conjectures, which cannot take the place of legal proof.
The defence version emerges as probable, consistent with medical evidence, and supported by an independent eye-witness, while the prosecution has failed to exclude reasonable alternative hypotheses.
In such circumstances, the statutory presumptions do not arise, and even otherwise, the benefit of doubt being a cornerstone of criminal jurisprudence must necessarily go to the accused.
